headline: Support Group Forms for People Who React to Their Own Posts
subheadline: Weekly meetings address shame cycle of self-liking and the 'it's for the algorithm' rationalization
summary: A Millbrook therapist has launched what may be the first support group specifically for people who compulsively like, react to, or comment on their own social media posts.
content:
The first rule of Self-Reactors Anonymous is that you don't react to the post announcing Self-Reactors Anonymous. Several founding members have already failed this rule.

"I told myself I was just testing that the like button worked," admitted Marcus, 29, during last week's inaugural meeting. "Then I told myself it was boosting the algorithm. Then I couldn't stop. I was commenting 'great point' on my own takes."

The support group, organized by therapist Dr. Linda Marsh, meets weekly in the basement of Millbrook Community Center. Attendance at the first session: 23 people. All of them admitted they had liked the MyFace event page for the meeting.

"Self-reacting exists on a spectrum," Dr. Marsh explained. "On one end, you have people who occasionally heart their own InstaSnap stories to see who's viewing. On the other end, we have individuals maintaining full conversations with themselves across multiple accounts."

The group uses a modified 12-step approach. Step one: admit you have reacted to your own post in the last 24 hours. At the first meeting, 847 self-reactions were collectively confessed.

"The shame is the hardest part," said attendee Jennifer, 34. "Everyone can see that you liked your own post. But there's this compulsion. You want that notification dopamine, even if you're the one creating it."

Some attendees developed elaborate justification systems. One member created a spreadsheet proving that self-liked posts performed better algorithmically. Another convinced themselves that the first like on any post should come from someone who truly appreciates the content, that being themselves.

The most severe case involved a man who created 12 alternate accounts solely to form what he called a "supportive audience" for his primary profile.

"They all had different personalities," he explained. "One was encouraging, one was critical but constructive. I spent more time managing my fake followers than actually posting."

Dr. Marsh emphasizes that the behavior, while embarrassing, is increasingly common in an attention economy.

"Social media has made external validation a measurable resource," she noted. "When that resource feels scarce, some people attempt to generate it themselves. It's a logical response to an illogical system."

The group plans to expand, with chapters forming in other cities. Organizers are carefully avoiding promoting it too heavily on social media.

"We don't want to attract people who would just like our posts," Dr. Marsh explained. "That would defeat the purpose."
author: Rachel Torres, Community Health
